svg.title: Medullary and anaplastic thyroid carcinoma, side by side
svg.desc: Schematic setting two different diseases side by side in two columns: medullary carcinoma on the left, anaplastic carcinoma on the right, separated by a dashed rule with no arrow of any kind between them. A grey band across the top states that three histologies mean three books, three years and three grading systems: the American Thyroid Association guideline that can still be cited for medullary carcinoma is the 2015 one, for anaplastic carcinoma it is the 2021 one, and the differentiated guideline was revised in 2025; this figure keeps the two guidelines separately named, and the sentences from the 2026 Latin American Thyroid Society consensus are not attributed to the American book. The left column is headed medullary carcinoma, where the clock runs in years, arising from the parafollicular C cells that lie between the follicles and secreting calcitonin and carcinoembryonic antigen. Its first cell, "one sentence, three consequences", says that radioiodine does nothing here because C cells do not take up iodine; that suppressing TSH is pointless because this disease does not grow to that signal, the tablet after surgery only replacing what the body needs; and that follow-up measures calcitonin and CEA rather than thyroglobulin. A red cell states that phaeochromocytoma must be excluded before the operation, quoting the 2015 American Thyroid Association guideline on medullary thyroid carcinoma verbatim: "a PHEO should be excluded prior to thyroidectomy". The explanation is that phaeochromocytoma sits in the adrenal gland and releases in bursts hormones that drive the blood pressure up, that the stimulus of anaesthesia and surgery can push the pressure to dangerous heights if it is still there, and that this is why an operation is often not booked the moment medullary carcinoma is diagnosed - the blood tests and the abdominal scan are not extras but the order things have to be done in. Next, why it turns up alongside medullary carcinoma: MEN2A is medullary carcinoma together with phaeochromocytoma, or with primary hyperparathyroidism, or with both; MEN2B is earlier in onset and more aggressive, and almost every carrier develops medullary carcinoma. The genetics are split into two cards. Germline RET can be passed on: about three quarters of medullary carcinomas are sporadic and one quarter hereditary, the hereditary ones nearly all arising from a germline RET mutation, autosomal dominant, with penetrance close to complete, and germline meaning every cell in the body carries it, that a blood test can find it, and that the question of passing it on exists at all. Somatic RET inside the tumour cannot be passed on: in roughly half of sporadic medullary carcinomas - different reviews write 50%, or 50% to 80% - a RET mutation is found in the tumour cells, a somatic mutation present only in that tumour and not passed to children. A yellow line adds that "half of medullary carcinomas carry a RET mutation" and "half of medullary carcinomas are hereditary" are two different sentences. The counselling cell quotes the guideline verbatim - "Genetic counseling and genetic testing for RET germline mutations should be offered to" - and notes that the same document also says patients with presumed sporadic disease should have testing for a germline RET mutation, because looking sporadic is not the same as being sporadic. What the counselling asks is set out: who in the family had what and at what age, particularly thyroid, adrenal and parathyroid; whether anyone had episodic high blood pressure, palpitations or sweating; whether anyone had thyroid surgery very young; and whether you have children or plan to. The guideline also lists pre-implantation or prenatal diagnostic testing, in those words, as an option to be discussed. The next cell quotes "The duty to warn a competent and capacitated patient" and explains that what is written is the doctor's duty to inform the patient, that the direction is that things are explained clearly to you rather than anyone being contacted on your behalf, that whether, when and whom to tell is yours to decide, and that this figure tells nobody to be tested. A further cell sets down plainly who carries the consequence of not testing, listing the three tiers by the position of the RET mutation: highest risk M918T, high risk codon 634, and other pathogenic variants moderate. For the high-risk tier the guideline sentence reads "Children in the ATA-H category should have a thyroidectomy performed at age 5 years or earlier"; for the moderate tier it is physical examination, neck ultrasound and calcitonin from the age of five; and for the highest tier it is earlier still, the guideline's own sentence being unobtainable so that a review is cited second-hand for surgery within the first year of life. The cell states that this is set down so that the reader knows what is behind that door, not as an instruction to knock on anybody's. The doubling time follows: what predicts is not one high reading but the doubling time. A French database followed 65 patients whose calcitonin was still abnormal after total thyroidectomy with bilateral neck dissection, drawn as three cards - doubling time under 6 months, 12 patients, 3 alive at five years (25%) and 1 at ten years (8%); 6 months to 2 years, 11/12 (92%) at five years and 3/8 (37%) at ten; longer than 2 years, 41 patients, all still alive at the end of the study. The note records that only doubling time was an independent predictor on multivariable analysis, that TNM stage and the EORTC score were significant on univariable analysis and stopped being significant once they entered the multivariable model, and that the figure has a boundary, being drawn from patients left with biochemical disease after surgery and not applicable to someone whose calcitonin became undetectable straight after the operation. A meta-analysis of ten studies adds that CEA doubling time predicts better than calcitonin, so both are measured, which is why nobody says "it has gone up" on the strength of one blood test. A further cell ties this to the pathological grade: calcitonin doubling time is 8.51 plus or minus 3.22 months in high grade against 38.42 plus or minus 11.19 months in low grade, and 66.7% of high-grade patients have a doubling time under one year against 1.0% of low-grade patients. A yellow cell records a guideline unrevised for eleven years: the citable guideline for medullary carcinoma is still the 2015 one, sixty-seven recommendations graded A to F on a system adapted from the US Preventive Services Task Force; eleven years is not nothing, since two selective RET inhibitors and one head-to-head phase III trial have arrived in the meantime, so a reader will meet "the guideline does not say this, but the doctors are discussing it", which is usually not the doctor going off-piste but the book not having been rewritten. The left column closes with Taiwan: in the national cancer registry report for 2023, medullary carcinoma accounted for 19 men and 29 women, 48 cases in all, 1.26% of male and 0.64% of female thyroid malignancies that year; survival data for medullary carcinoma in Taiwan and the hereditary share return no entry; and which drug is reimbursed in Taiwan for which thyroid cancer is not on this figure, the rules being transcribed verbatim in the sister article, "How this goes in Taiwan". The right column is headed anaplastic carcinoma, where the clock runs in weeks: other sections are about months and years, and this column is about this week. A red quotation carries recommendation 1 of the 2026 Latin American Thyroid Society expert panel consensus verbatim - "A rapidly enlarging thyroid mass should be considered a medical emergency and managed accordingly." - with "should" meaning unanimous agreement. The next cell explains that this consensus ties its wording to its votes: "should" is unanimous agreement, "is recommended" at least seventy per cent, and "may be considered" under seventy per cent or dependent on local resources. The other book is the 2021 American Thyroid Association guideline on anaplastic carcinoma, thirty-one recommendations plus sixteen good practice statements on the American College of Physicians grading system; the years and the grading systems differ, so the figure names them separately. The airway section states first that the introduction of a 17-patient case series records that more than three in ten cases of anaplastic thyroid cancer "may present" with acute airway obstruction, marking that as a background generalisation rather than a rate calculated from those 17 people, and that this is why "should a tracheostomy be done first" is usually raised in the first days after diagnosis. It then quotes "Elective tracheostomy should not be routinely performed." and labels it as recommendation 23 of the 2026 Latin American Thyroid Society consensus, with "should" and unanimous agreement. The next cell says plainly that the 2021 American Thyroid Association guideline does not carry this as a recommendation - a full-text index was searched and none of the phrasings hit; it discusses tracheostomy among the elements of a decision, saying it relieves upper airway obstruction immediately but requires a great deal of care education, and it does carry a separate recommendation that the vocal cords be assessed at every patient's first visit - so "do not do an elective tracheostomy" is not attributed to the American book here, being the Latin American consensus speaking. The reasoning cell records that tracheostomy markedly reduces quality of life, does little to lengthen survival, and that bleeding and tumour growing out through the stoma are both common complications, which is why thinking has changed over the past decade, while the same passage writes the other half too: what may have to be done if acute respiratory distress occurs must be discussed in advance. A figure cell gives emergency tracheostomy for symptomatic airway obstruction a 30-day mortality of 17.6%, from 17 consecutive patients at one hospital over two years with median overall survival 11 months and one-year survival 36%, the authors adding that it should not be attempted under local anaesthesia on the ward or in the emergency department but in theatre by an experienced head and neck surgeon. A grey line closes the section: put the two halves together and that is its real shape - not routinely done in advance, and not first discussed at the moment of suffocation, the conversation having to be finished while the patient is awake, able to speak, and with family present. The BRAF section quotes recommendation 6 of the same consensus verbatim - "Rapid BRAF V600E testing should be performed as soon as possible after diagnosis (ideally within 24 hours) when targeted therapies are available and timely testing is feasible." - again "should" and unanimous. Why the hurry: because the result changes what is done that week; the pooled prevalence of BRAF V600E in anaplastic carcinoma is 33%, with individual studies ranging from 0% to 93%, so about six in ten tumours do not carry it, and the two figures do not conflict, one being a pooled value and the other the clinical reality of one centre. It is technically possible: one group ran digital polymerase chain reaction on fine-needle aspirate and had results back within twenty-four hours for two patients, a case report of two people rather than routine practice. Survival is drawn as two cards side by side. The left is labelled historical and reads "median survival four months", with a note that the source writes "historically", meaning that this is how it used to be and that it is a figure from the past. The right is labelled recent cohort and reads "median overall survival 9.5 months", with a note that the study writing that sentence is itself data on 479 patients with anaplastic carcinoma at one large medical centre between 2000 and 2019, whose median overall survival across the whole cohort was 0.79 years, that is 9.5 months. Below, the same cohort is read by era for one- and two-year survival: the 227 patients from 2000 to 2013 reached 35% and 18%, and the 152 patients from 2017 to 2019 reached 59% and 42%, with a hazard ratio between the eras of 0.50 (95% confidence interval 0.38 to 0.67), and a note that this is one hospital's figure and not a world average. A further cell places two more beside them: 97 patients at another academic hospital between 2000 and 2021, median overall survival 6.5 months (confidence interval 4.3 to 10.0), and a Spanish and Portuguese registry of 214 patients at 4.5 months; the differences coming from the era, from whether that hospital can complete molecular testing and start treatment within days, and from the extent of disease at diagnosis, anaplastic carcinoma always being stage IV with only the letter A, B or C varying. The right column closes with Taiwan: in the national cancer registry report for 2023, anaplastic carcinoma accounted for 22 men and 30 women, 52 cases in all, and survival and treatment data for anaplastic carcinoma in Taiwan return no entry in the official statistics. The figure ends with a red-bordered block headed "This figure will not mix the two columns, and it tells nobody to be tested", holding four statements: these are two columns because they are two diseases, the calcitonin and doubling time on the left cannot be carried across and the clock that runs in weeks on the right cannot be carried back, and no arrow joins them; "Elective tracheostomy should not be routinely performed" is recommendation 23 of the 2026 Latin American Thyroid Society consensus while the 2021 American Thyroid Association guideline does not carry it as a recommendation, and this figure keeps the names apart; the genetics cell describes what counselling asks and the word the guideline uses, which is "offered", so the figure does not tell anyone to ask a relative to be tested, what the guideline writes being the doctor's duty to inform the patient rather than to make contact on their behalf; and which drug is reimbursed in Taiwan for which thyroid cancer appears in neither column, the rules being transcribed verbatim in the sister article, "How this goes in Taiwan". A closing cell carries one sentence from each column to be said out loud first: for medullary carcinoma, before surgery, has the phaeochromocytoma question been tested for and what was the result; and for anaplastic carcinoma, has BRAF V600E been sent, on what day, and roughly when does it come back.

g.text: TWO DIFFERENT DISEASES - DIFFERENT CELLS, DIFFERENT CLOCKS, DIFFERENT GUIDELINES
Medullary and anaplastic carcinoma: two thyroid cancers
that are not "thyroid cancer"
Neither of these is the disease most people read about online. They arise from different cells, are followed with different
numbers, are covered by different guidelines, and are even measured in different units of time.
On the left, medullary carcinoma, where the clock runs in years and the story is two tumour markers and one gene. On the right,
anaplastic carcinoma, where the clock runs in weeks and the story is the airway and one blood sample that has to leave the
building. No arrow joins the two columns.
Three histologies, three books, three years, three grading systems
The American Thyroid Association guideline that can still be cited for medullary carcinoma is the 2015 one; for anaplastic carcinoma it is the 2021 one;
the differentiated guideline was revised in 2025.
This figure keeps the two columns apart and keeps the two guidelines separately named - the sentences from the 2026 Latin American Thyroid Society
consensus are not attributed to the American book.
Left column - medullary carcinoma, where the
clock runs in years
It arises from the parafollicular C cells lying between the follicles, and what
they secrete is calcitonin and carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA).
One sentence, three consequences
Radioiodine does nothing here, because C cells do not take up iodine.
Suppressing TSH is pointless, because this disease does not grow to that
signal - the tablet after surgery only replaces what the body needs.
Follow-up does not measure thyroglobulin. It measures calcitonin and CEA.
Before the operation, phaeochromocytoma must be excluded
Phaeochromocytoma sits in the adrenal gland and releases, in bursts,
hormones that drive the blood pressure up. If it is still there, the
stimulus of anaesthesia and surgery can push the pressure to
dangerous heights.
That is why an operation is often not booked the moment medullary
carcinoma is diagnosed. Those blood tests and that abdominal scan are
not extras; they are the order things have to be done in.
“a PHEO should be excluded prior to thyroidectomy”
Verbatim from the 2015 American Thyroid Association guideline on medullary thyroid
carcinoma.
Why it turns up alongside medullary carcinoma
MEN2A
Medullary carcinoma together with phaeochromocytoma, or with
primary hyperparathyroidism, or with both.
MEN2B
Earlier in onset and more aggressive; almost every carrier
develops medullary carcinoma.
The genetics: keep the two kinds of mutation apart
Germline RET (can be passed on)
About three quarters of medullary carcinomas are sporadic and one quarter
hereditary; the hereditary ones nearly all come from a germline mutation in
RET, autosomal dominant, with penetrance close to complete. "Germline"
means every cell in the body carries it, that a blood test can find it, and that the
question of passing it on exists at all.
Somatic RET inside the tumour (cannot be passed on)
In roughly half of sporadic medullary carcinomas - different reviews write
50%, or 50% to 80% - a RET mutation can be found in the tumour cells. That is a
somatic mutation present only in that tumour, and it is not passed to children.
"Half of medullary carcinomas carry a RET mutation" and "half of
medullary carcinomas are hereditary" are two different sentences.
What genetic counselling asks, and the word "offered"
“Genetic counseling and genetic testing for RET germline mutations
should be offered to”
Verbatim from the 2015 American Thyroid Association guideline on medullary thyroid
carcinoma. The same document also says "Patients with presumed sporadic MTC
should have genetic testing to detect a germline RET mutation" - because looking
sporadic is not the same as being sporadic.
Roughly what the counselling asks
Who in the family had what, and at what age, particularly thyroid, adrenal
and parathyroid.
Whether anyone had episodic high blood pressure, palpitations or sweating.
Whether anyone had thyroid surgery very young.
Whether you have children, and whether you plan to.
The guideline also lists pre-implantation or prenatal diagnostic testing, in those
words, as an option to be discussed.
On whether the family should be told, here is what the guideline
actually says
“The duty to warn a competent and capacitated patient”
Verbatim from the 2015 American Thyroid Association guideline on medullary thyroid
carcinoma.
What is written is the doctor's duty to inform the patient. The direction
is that things are explained clearly to you, not that anyone is contacted
on your behalf.
Whether to tell, when to tell and whom to tell is yours to decide, and
you may take your time. This figure tells nobody to be tested.
Who carries the consequence of not testing is also written
down plainly
Highest risk
M918T
High risk
Codon 634
Moderate
Other pathogenic variants
For the high-risk tier the sentence reads "Children in the ATA-H category
should have a thyroidectomy performed at age 5 years or earlier"; for the
moderate tier it is physical examination, neck ultrasound and calcitonin from
the age of five; and for the highest tier it is earlier still - the guideline's own
sentence could not be obtained, so a review is cited second-hand for surgery
within the first year of life. This is set down so that you know what is behind
that door, not as an instruction to knock on anybody's.
What predicts is not one high reading, it is the doubling time
A French database followed 65 patients whose calcitonin was still abnormal after total
thyroidectomy with bilateral neck dissection.
Doubling time under 6 months
12 patients
Alive at five years
Alive at ten years
6 months to 2 years
Alive at five years
Alive at ten years
Longer than 2 years
41 patients
At the end of the study
All still alive
On multivariable analysis only doubling time was an independent predictor; TNM
stage and the EORTC score were significant on univariable analysis and stopped
being significant once they entered the multivariable model. The figure has a
boundary: these are patients left with biochemical disease after surgery, and it
cannot be applied to someone whose calcitonin became undetectable straight after
the operation.
A meta-analysis of ten studies adds one line: CEA doubling time predicts better than
calcitonin, so both are measured. Which is why nobody says "it has gone up" on the
strength of one blood test.
It is tied to the pathological grade as well
Calcitonin doubling time in high grade
8.51 plus or minus 3.22 months
In low grade
38.42 plus or minus 11.19 months
High grade, doubling time under one year
Low grade, doubling time under one year
A guideline that has not been revised for eleven years
The American Thyroid Association guideline that can still be cited for
medullary carcinoma is the 2015 one, sixty-seven recommendations,
graded A to F on a system adapted from the US Preventive Services
Task Force.
Eleven years is not nothing: two selective RET inhibitors and one
head-to-head phase III trial have arrived since. So you will meet "the
guideline does not say this, but the doctors are discussing it", and that
is usually not the doctor going off-piste; it is the book not having been
rewritten.
Taiwan (medullary carcinoma)
In the national cancer registry report for 2023, medullary carcinoma
accounted for 19 men and 29 women, 48 cases in all, 1.26% of male and
0.64% of female thyroid malignancies that year.
Survival data for medullary carcinoma in Taiwan, and what share of cases
is hereditary, return no entry - not because nobody looked, but because the
report has no such item.
Which drug is reimbursed in Taiwan for which thyroid cancer is not on this
figure; the rules are transcribed verbatim in the sister article, "How this
goes in Taiwan".
Right column - anaplastic carcinoma, where the
clock runs in weeks
Other sections are about what happens in months or years. This column is
about this week.
“A rapidly enlarging thyroid mass should be considered a medical
emergency and managed accordingly.”
Verbatim, recommendation 1 of the 2026 Latin American Thyroid Society expert panel
consensus; "should" means unanimous agreement.
This consensus ties its wording to its votes
should
Unanimous agreement
is recommended
At least seventy per cent
may be considered
Under seventy per cent, or dependent on local
resources
The other book is the 2021 American Thyroid Association guideline on
anaplastic carcinoma, thirty-one recommendations plus sixteen good practice
statements, on the American College of Physicians grading system. The years
and the grading systems differ, so this figure names them separately.
The airway: this cell says it straight
The introduction of a 17-patient case series states that more than three in
ten cases of anaplastic thyroid cancer "may present" with acute airway
obstruction - that is a background generalisation, not a rate calculated from
those 17 people. It is why "should a tracheostomy be done first" is usually
raised in the first days after diagnosis.
“Elective tracheostomy should not be routinely performed.”
Verbatim, recommendation 23 of the 2026 Latin American Thyroid Society expert
panel consensus; "should" means unanimous agreement.
The 2021 American Thyroid Association guideline does not
carry this as a recommendation
A full-text index was searched and none of the phrasings hit. It discusses
tracheostomy among the elements of a decision, saying that it relieves upper
airway obstruction immediately but requires a great deal of care education; it
does carry a separate recommendation that the vocal cords be assessed at
every patient's first visit.
So "do not do an elective tracheostomy" is not attributed to the American book
here. It is the Latin American consensus speaking.
The reasoning is in the text: tracheostomy markedly reduces quality of life,
does little to lengthen survival, and bleeding and tumour growing out through
the stoma are both common complications, which is why thinking has changed
over the past decade.
But the same passage writes the other half too: what may have to be done if
acute respiratory distress occurs must be discussed in advance.
Emergency tracheostomy for symptomatic airway obstruction
30-day mortality 17.6%
That figure comes from 17 consecutive patients at one hospital over two years,
median overall survival 11 months and one-year survival 36%. The authors add
that it should not be attempted under local anaesthesia on the ward or in the
emergency department, but in theatre by an experienced head and neck
surgeon.
Put the two halves together and that is the real shape of this section: not
routinely done in advance, and not first discussed at the moment of
suffocation. The conversation has to be finished while the patient is
awake, able to speak, and with family present.
How fast that blood sample leaves the building
“Rapid BRAF V600E testing should be performed as soon as possible
after diagnosis (ideally within 24 hours) when targeted therapies are
available and timely testing is feasible.”
Verbatim, recommendation 6 of the 2026 Latin American Thyroid Society expert panel
consensus; "should" again, and unanimous.
Why the hurry
Because the result changes what is done that week. The pooled prevalence of
BRAF V600E in anaplastic carcinoma is 33%, with individual studies ranging
from 0% to 93%; put the other way, about six in ten tumours do not carry it. The
two figures do not conflict: one is a pooled value, the other is the clinical
reality of one centre.
It is technically possible: one group ran digital polymerase chain reaction on
fine-needle aspirate and had results back within twenty-four hours for two
patients - a case report of two people, not routine practice.
The survival figures have to carry their era, because they have
changed
Historical

four months

meaning that this is how it used to
be. It is a figure from the past.

survival 9.5
months

is itself data on 479 patients with
anaplastic carcinoma treated at one
large medical centre between 2000
and 2019; median overall survival
across the whole cohort was 0.79
years, that is 9.5 months.
What matters more is reading it by era (one- and two-year
survival)

One year
Two years
Between the two eras the hazard ratio is 0.50 (95% confidence interval 0.38 to
0.67). This is one hospital's figure, not a world average.
Four figures side by side are more accurate than any one of
them alone
97 patients at another academic
hospital, 2000 to 2021
Median overall survival 6.5 months
(confidence interval 4.3 to 10.0)

214 patients

The differences come from the era, from whether that hospital can complete
molecular testing and start treatment within days, and from the extent of
disease at diagnosis - anaplastic carcinoma is always stage IV, and what
varies is the letter A, B or C.
Taiwan (anaplastic carcinoma)
In the national cancer registry report for 2023, anaplastic carcinoma
accounted for 22 men and 30 women, 52 cases in all.
Survival and treatment data for anaplastic carcinoma in Taiwan return no
entry in the official statistics.
This figure will not mix the two columns, and it tells nobody to be tested
These are two columns because they are two diseases. The calcitonin and the doubling time on the left cannot be carried across, and the clock that
runs in weeks on the right cannot be carried back. No arrow joins them.
"Elective tracheostomy should not be routinely performed" is recommendation 23 of the 2026 Latin American Thyroid Society consensus; the 2021
American Thyroid Association guideline does not carry it as a recommendation. This figure keeps the names apart.
The genetics cell describes what counselling asks and the word the guideline uses, which is "offered" - offered, and explained. This figure does not tell
you to ask any relative to be tested; what the guideline writes is the doctor's duty to inform the patient, not to make contact on their behalf.
Which drug is reimbursed in Taiwan for which thyroid cancer appears in neither column; the rules are transcribed verbatim in the sister article,
"How this goes in Taiwan".
One sentence from each column, to be said out loud first
Medullary: "Before surgery, has the phaeochromocytoma question been tested for? What was the result?"
Anaplastic: "Has BRAF V600E been sent? On what day? Roughly when does it come back?"
Schematic, redrawn from the 2015 American Thyroid Association guideline on medullary thyroid carcinoma, the 2026 Latin American Thyroid Society expert
panel consensus on anaplastic thyroid cancer, the 2021 American Thyroid Association guideline on anaplastic thyroid cancer, the 2005 study of calcitonin and
carcinoembryonic antigen doubling times, the meta-analysis of doubling times and the study of tumour grade, the 2020 analysis of overall survival in 479 patients
with anaplastic carcinoma, two single-institution anaplastic cohorts, the emergency tracheostomy series and the Taiwan national cancer registry report for 2023;
not reproduced from the figures of the original papers. The cohorts, designs and endpoints of the underlying studies differ, so the data points must not be compared
directly.
